title: 300 complaints in 20 minutes, one shape
explain:
On a weekday morning between 09:12 and 09:32, a contact centre receives more than 300 complaints with the same shape.
Customers report a debit that does not match the payment status shown in the app, or a credit they expected that has not appeared.
Three hundred voices, one pattern, and no incident bridge yet.

Here's how that happens:

→ Complaints arrive with the same shape
→ Debits do not match the app status
→ Expected credits have not appeared

The assumption was:
"Find the root cause first, then protect the customers."

Start with an incident bridge that separates three workstreams: customer and financial containment, technical root cause analysis, and communications. Containment owns the affected-transaction register, the decision on the next batch and any remediation, while the other workstreams proceed in parallel, so that customers are protected even before the root cause is known.

Protect customers before you understand the cause.

BA Takeaway

Open the bridge and split the work. Containment owns the register and the next-batch decision. Root cause and communications run in parallel. Customers are protected while the cause is still unknown.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer and financial containment
→ Technical root cause analysis
→ Communications

The real requirement isn't "What caused it?"

It's "What evidence proves which customers are affected, and what protects them right now?"

Have you ever seen 300 identical complaints land in 20 minutes and known it was one incident, not 300?
takeaway: Containment owns the affected-transaction register, the decision on the next batch and any remediation, while the other workstreams proceed in parallel.

title: UPI, cards, net banking and wallets all failing on the same day
explain:
On the same day, UPI payments fail with timeouts, card payments fail at the gateway, net banking sessions drop before confirmation, and wallet payments fail after the wallet is debited.
Four rails, four failure shapes, one very bad day.
Is it one cause, or several?

Here's how that happens:

→ UPI payments time out
→ Card payments fail at the gateway
→ Net banking sessions drop before confirmation
→ Wallet payments fail after the wallet is debited

The assumption was:
"One bad day means one cause."

Build one incident table segmented by rail and channel, gateway, bank, response code, time window and transaction state, and join each row to its ledger and clearing evidence by correlation ID. For each segment, establish whether the payment left the customer account, whether it reached clearing or the scheme, and what its authoritative state is now. Segmenting the incident this way shows whether there is one cause or several, which decides whether one fix or several are needed.

Segment first. One cause or several, the evidence decides.

BA Takeaway

One table, segmented by rail, and every row joined to its ledger and clearing evidence by correlation ID. For each segment ask the same three questions: did it leave the account, did it reach clearing, and what is its authoritative state now.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Rail and channel
→ Gateway and bank
→ Response code and time window
→ Transaction state
→ Ledger and clearing evidence

The real requirement isn't "What failed?"

It's "What evidence proves, per segment, where each payment stopped?"

Have you ever had four rails fail at once and had to prove it was not one single cause?
takeaway: Segmenting the incident this way shows whether there is one cause or several, which decides whether one fix or several are needed.

title: The retailer, the bank API and the missing outcome
explain:
A retailer wants its checkout connected directly to a bank's payment API, so orders can be paid without leaving the retailer's site.
On a EUR 60,000 day of orders, the question is not how to call the API.
It is how the retailer learns whether each payment actually completed.

Here's how that happens:

→ Retailer submits payment instructions to the bank API
→ Bank returns a response
→ Retailer must learn the final outcome
→ Order is created only when the outcome is known

The assumption was:
"An API is just endpoints."

Walk through the integration in layers and make each layer testable, starting with the contract, the endpoints, the request and response schemas, mandatory and optional fields, validation rules and error codes, then the authentication, the asynchronous status path and the recovery procedures. An acceptance response is never completion, and the retailer needs a status enquiry path for every payment whose outcome is unclear.

A payment API is a promise about outcomes, not a list of fields.

BA Takeaway

Define the contract first: what each response promises, what the caller does next, how the final outcome is learned, how failures are handled and how the integration is monitored. Every layer is testable on its own.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Contract and schemas
→ Authentication
→ Asynchronous status path
→ Failure handling and recovery
→ Monitoring

The real requirement isn't "Can we call the API?"

It's "What evidence proves each payment completed, and what do we do when the outcome is unclear?"

Have you ever integrated an API that answered every call, yet never told you whether the payment completed?
takeaway: Walk through the integration in layers and make each layer testable, starting with the contract, then the authentication, the asynchronous status path and the recovery procedures.

title: Fast, secure, easy: the gateway brief with no requirements
explain:
A retailer sells online and in store and wants a third-party payment gateway for card and instant payments at checkout.
The requirements are three words: fast, secure and easy to integrate.
Three words, and no one can build from them.

Here's how that happens:

→ Retailer wants card and instant payments at checkout
→ Brief says fast, secure and easy
→ No methods, currencies, channels or journeys defined

The assumption was:
"Fast, secure and easy is a requirement."

Start from the customer and finance outcomes, not from the provider brochure: list the payment methods, currencies, channels and customer journeys in scope, and for each one define the expected flow, authorisation, capture, refund, partial refund, void, chargeback handling and settlement timing. Then define the API capabilities, the request and response contracts, the error handling, the security, the retries and the reconciliation, so the provider can be compared on evidence rather than on marketing.

A wish is not a requirement. An outcome is.

BA Takeaway

Define every journey before talking to a provider: flow, authorisation, capture, refund, void, chargeback handling and settlement timing, then the API capabilities, error handling, security, retries and reconciliation. Providers are compared on evidence, not on marketing.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Payment methods and currencies
→ Channels and customer journeys
→ Authorisation, capture, refund, void, chargeback
→ Settlement timing
→ API capabilities and reconciliation

The real requirement isn't "Which gateway is best?"

It's "What evidence proves a provider meets each journey's outcome?"

Have you ever been handed a brief that was three adjectives and told to write requirements from it?
takeaway: Define the API capabilities, the request and response contracts, the error handling, the security, the retries and the reconciliation, so the provider can be compared on evidence rather than on marketing.

title: SIT passed clean. Production failed on day one.
explain:
A merchant payment API integration passes system integration testing cleanly, every test case returning the expected response.
It fails in production on day one.
The same calls, the same payloads, and a failure rate climbing by the hour.

Here's how that happens:

→ SIT passes every test case
→ Production fails from the first submissions
→ Failure rate is rising

The assumption was:
"If it passed SIT, production is the same."

Contain the impact first by stopping new submissions if the failure rate is rising, telling the partner what is known and what is not, and confirming which payments have a financial effect and which do not. Then compare the environments side by side in a fixed order: endpoint and configuration, credentials and scopes, certificates and expiry dates, network routes and firewall rules, feature flags, downstream dependency versions and production data. The difference between test and production is usually in one of these, and comparing them in a fixed order finds it faster than guessing.

SIT and production are two different systems that happen to share a name.

BA Takeaway

Contain first, then compare the environments in a fixed order. Endpoint and configuration, credentials and certificates, network and firewall, flags and dependencies, then production data. Guessing is slower than comparing.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Endpoint and configuration
→ Credentials, scopes and certificates
→ Network routes and firewall rules
→ Feature flags and dependency versions
→ Production data

The real requirement isn't "Did SIT pass?"

It's "What evidence proves the two environments match, and which payments have a financial effect?"

Have you ever watched a clean SIT build fail in production and had to prove the environments were never the same?
takeaway: The difference between test and production is usually in one of these, and comparing them in a fixed order finds it faster than guessing.

title: HTTP 200, order unpaid, account debited
explain:
A fintech partner integrates with a bank's payment API to submit customer credit transfers for its merchants.
In testing, the API returns a successful HTTP response, but the merchant's downstream order record is not created.
In one case the payment is debited while the merchant dashboard still shows the order as unpaid.

Here's how that happens:

→ API returns HTTP 200
→ Merchant order record is not created
→ Payment debited, dashboard shows unpaid

The assumption was:
"HTTP 200 means the payment completed."

Start from the contract, not from the code: the API definition must state, for each endpoint, what a success response promises, receipt, validation, acceptance or completion, and what the caller must do next in each case. Then review authentication, schema, mandatory fields, business validation, response codes, idempotency and observability, because a success response that promises completion when it only means receipt will mislead every caller.

A 200 can mean receipt. It never means completion unless the contract says so.

BA Takeaway

State what success promises per endpoint, and what the caller must do next in each case. Then review authentication, schema, mandatory fields, business validation, response codes, idempotency and observability, because a misleading success will mislead every caller.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Receipt
→ Validation
→ Acceptance
→ Completion

The real requirement isn't "Did the API return 200?"

It's "What evidence proves what that 200 promised, and what must the caller do next?"

Have you ever seen a 200 response debited an account while the order stayed unpaid?
takeaway: A success response that promises completion when it only means receipt will mislead every caller.

title: The API contract that forgot to say what success means
explain:
A bank is publishing a Payment API for corporate customers and retail partners.
The first draft of the contract is a list of fields with no rules.
It does not say which fields are required, what happens when a field is missing, which error code means what, whether a success response means the payment completed, or how a caller should safely retry.
A list of fields, and EUR 100,000 a day will flow through it.

Here's how that happens:

→ Contract drafted as a list of fields
→ No required or optional rules
→ No error code meanings
→ No statement of what success means
→ No safe retry rule

The assumption was:
"A list of fields is a contract."

Define every field with its name, type, cardinality, validation rule and error code, and state explicitly which fields are required, which are optional, and which are conditionally mandatory by rail, destination or product. Where a field is optional under the message schema but the bank's reporting or product needs it, say so in the contract and state the source the bank will use and the derivation rule.

If success is undefined, every caller will define it differently.

BA Takeaway

A contract states what success promises, what each error means, and how to retry safely. Every field carries its name, type, cardinality, validation rule and error code, and conditionally mandatory fields are named by rail, destination and product.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field definition
→ Required and optional fields
→ Conditionally mandatory fields
→ Bank-needed optional fields
→ Success response meaning
→ Safe retry rule

The real requirement isn't "What fields does the API take?"

It's "What evidence proves a caller can use this API without guessing?"

Have you ever read an API contract that listed every field and answered none of the real questions?
takeaway: Where a field is optional under the message schema but the bank's reporting or product needs it, say so in the contract and state the source the bank will use and the derivation rule.

title: Two weeks to build a Payment API integration
explain:
A retailer needs a Payment API integration delivered in a two-week sprint.
The checkout must submit payment instructions to the bank, receive a clear acceptance or rejection, and create the order only when the payment outcome is known.
Two weeks, and the contract is still unwritten.

Here's how that happens:

→ Sprint starts, two weeks on the clock
→ Checkout must submit instructions to the bank
→ Order created only when the outcome is known

The assumption was:
"Start building, the contract can follow."

Start the sprint with discovery compressed into the first two days: confirm the business outcome, the checkout journey, the payment types in scope, the expected volumes and the response contract. The contract definition matters most, so agree in writing what each response means, so that an acceptance response is never mistaken for completion, and define the status enquiry path the retailer uses when a payment outcome is unclear.

The contract is the build. Everything else is typing.

BA Takeaway

Discovery takes two days, and the contract is agreed in writing before building starts. Acceptance is never mistaken for completion, and the status enquiry path is defined for every unclear outcome.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Business outcome and journey
→ Payment types and volumes
→ Response contract in writing
→ Status enquiry path

The real requirement isn't "Can we build it in two weeks?"

It's "What evidence proves the contract is agreed before a line of code is written?"

Have you ever started a two-week build with the contract still unwritten?
takeaway: The contract definition matters most, so agree in writing what each response means, so that an acceptance response is never mistaken for completion.

title: Customers start onboarding, then vanish at document upload
explain:
A bank wants more new retail customers to complete digital onboarding, but only a small share of started applications reach an active account.
Customers abandon the journey at document upload and at identity verification.
Many who do finish are later held for manual review because documents are unclear or data does not match.

Here's how that happens:

→ Application started
→ Identity details entered
→ Document upload, customers abandon here
→ Identity verification, more abandon here
→ Manual review holds the rest
→ Account opened, first transaction rare

The assumption was:
"Customers abandon because they are not interested."

Start with evidence, not opinions, and measure the funnel stage by stage: started, identity details entered, document uploaded, identity verified, screening complete, account opened and first transaction. Then map the friction, the document collection, the validation, the screening, the exception handling and the conversion measures, so the redesign targets the stages where customers actually drop off.

Measure the funnel. Opinions do not fix drop-off.

BA Takeaway

Measure every stage before redesigning anything. The funnel shows where customers actually leave, and the redesign targets those stages, not the ones the team guesses about.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Started
→ Identity details entered
→ Document uploaded
→ Identity verified
→ Screening complete
→ Account opened and first transaction

The real requirement isn't "Why do customers leave?"

It's "What evidence proves at which stage they leave, and what blocks them there?"

Have you ever watched a funnel and found the drop-off was at a stage nobody had blamed?
takeaway: Map the friction, the document collection, the validation, the screening, the exception handling and the conversion measures, so the redesign targets the stages where customers actually drop off.

title: SCT Inst has no maximum, 10 seconds, payee check mandatory
explain:
A bank must change its instant euro payments to match the current scheme rules.
There is no longer a scheme-level maximum amount for SCT Inst, execution must complete within 10 seconds, and verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments.
The change touches the mobile app, the payment engine, the sanctions and fraud services, the clearing adapter, the ledger and the customer notifications.
Six systems, one scheme change.

Here's how that happens:

→ Scheme rules change: no maximum, 10 seconds, payee verification
→ Mobile app, engine, sanctions, fraud, clearing, ledger and notifications all affected

The assumption was:
"It is a small scheme change."

Build the impact analysis as a map, not as a list of opinions: start from the change and walk upstream to find which channels, products and customer journeys can submit an instant euro payment, which limits and validations apply today, and which of those must change, then walk downstream to find the systems, data, interfaces, controls, tests, operations and release dependencies that are affected.

A scheme change is a map, not a ticket.

BA Takeaway

Walk upstream from the change to every channel, product and journey that can submit an instant euro payment, then walk downstream to every system, interface, control, test and release dependency. The map is the impact analysis.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Channels and products upstream
→ Limits and validations today
→ Systems and interfaces downstream
→ Controls, tests and release dependencies

The real requirement isn't "What changed in the scheme?"

It's "What evidence proves every affected channel, system and control has been found?"

Have you ever scoped a scheme change as small, then found it touched six systems?
takeaway: Build the impact analysis as a map, not as a list of opinions: start from the change and walk upstream, then walk downstream.

title: One day to go-live, compliance finds a missing requirement
explain:
A bank is one day from deploying an upgrade to its instant euro payment service.
UAT is signed off, regression evidence is filed, the deployment window is booked and the customer communications are ready.
Late in the afternoon the compliance team raises a requirement nobody recorded: verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments.

Here's how that happens:

→ UAT signed off, deployment booked
→ Compliance raises an unrecorded requirement
→ One day to go-live

The assumption was:
"UAT sign-off means the requirements are complete."

First classify the item precisely as a defect against an agreed requirement, a safety or compliance obligation, or genuinely new scope, and confirm the obligation at its source, for example verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments from 9 October 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/886, and SCT Inst execution has a 10-second maximum with no scheme-level maximum since the 2025 rulebook change. Then triage defect versus new scope, quantify the risk and obtain a formal go or no-go decision, because a mandatory compliance obligation cannot be deferred the way new scope can.

A mandatory obligation cannot be deferred like new scope.

BA Takeaway

Classify first, then triage. A defect against an agreed requirement, a safety or compliance obligation, or genuinely new scope, each takes a different path, and a mandatory obligation ends in a formal go or no-go decision, never a quiet deferral.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Defect against an agreed requirement
→ Safety or compliance obligation
→ Genuinely new scope
→ Risk quantification
→ Formal go or no-go decision

The real requirement isn't "Can we still deploy tomorrow?"

It's "What evidence proves what this item is, and who formally decided?"

Have you ever had a mandatory requirement surface the day before go-live?
takeaway: Triage defect versus new scope, quantify the risk and obtain a formal go or no-go decision, because a mandatory compliance obligation cannot be deferred the way new scope can.

title: UAT morning one: most collections rejected
explain:
A bank is starting user acceptance testing for a new SEPA direct debit collection service.
On the first morning the failure rate is critical: most test collections are rejected, mandate references cannot be found, and the test schedule shows collections submitted on the wrong day.
The testers are ready. The environment is not.

Here's how that happens:

→ UAT starts for SEPA direct debit collections
→ Most test collections rejected
→ Mandate references cannot be found
→ Collections submitted on the wrong day

The assumption was:
"Testers should push through and log the failures."

Begin with a triage that separates the failure causes into four buckets, environment, test data, build and requirements, and check the environment first: whether the UAT build is the intended version, whether the endpoints, credentials and scheme adapters point at the right test systems, and whether the feature flags are set as the release notes state. Only then decide whether to continue, fix and restart, or stop, because continuing a test on a broken environment wastes the testers' time and produces evidence that cannot be trusted.

Evidence from a broken environment is not evidence.

BA Takeaway

Triage into four buckets and check the environment first: build version, endpoints, credentials, adapters and flags. Only then decide whether to continue, fix and restart, or stop.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Environment
→ Test data
→ Build
→ Requirements

The real requirement isn't "How many tests failed?"

It's "What evidence proves the environment was fit to test in the first place?"

Have you ever watched a UAT day burn on an environment that was never the right build?
takeaway: Only then decide whether to continue, fix and restart, or stop, because continuing a test on a broken environment wastes the testers' time and produces evidence that cannot be trusted.

steps.note: Environment, test data, build and requirements.

title: A few customers, one wrong EMI
explain:
A bank receives complaints from a small group of loan customers that their monthly EMI is wrong.
Most customers are unaffected, which makes the problem harder, not easier.
A handful of complaints, and a calculation that is wrong for some loans and right for the rest.

Here's how that happens:

→ Small group complains the EMI is wrong
→ Most customers unaffected
→ Complaints share no obvious pattern

The assumption was:
"Only the complainers are affected."

Start by defining the affected population precisely: list every complaining account and search for others with the same characteristics, so the fix covers silent cases as well as complaints. For each affected loan, capture the full calculation inputs: principal, sanctioned rate, rate change history with effective dates, tenure, schedule generation rules, rounding policy, part-payment history and customer data. The pattern only emerges when the cases are compared, because the affected loans share a characteristic, such as a particular rate change date, that the unaffected loans do not.

The pattern only emerges when the cases are compared.

BA Takeaway

Define the population first, including the silent cases, then capture every calculation input per loan and compare. The affected loans share a characteristic the unaffected ones do not, and the comparison is what finds it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Complaining accounts
→ Silent cases with the same characteristics
→ Calculation inputs per loan
→ Rate change history and effective dates

The real requirement isn't "Which customers complained?"

It's "What evidence proves who else is affected, and what the affected loans share?"

Have you ever found a defect that only hit a few customers, and the silent cases were the real problem?
takeaway: The pattern only emerges when the cases are compared, because the affected loans share a characteristic, such as a particular rate change date, that the unaffected loans do not.

title: Make payments faster: the brief with no user, no baseline, no target
explain:
A bank wants to launch an instant payment product for small business customers.
The sponsor has asked the team to make payments faster.
The request has no named user group, no baseline, no target speed and no statement of the problem customers actually face today.
Faster than what, for whom, and by when? Nobody can say.

Here's how that happens:

→ Sponsor asks for faster payments
→ No user group named
→ No baseline and no target speed
→ No statement of the customer problem

The assumption was:
"Faster is a requirement."

Start by naming the target users precisely, for example small businesses that pay domestic suppliers on fixed weekly cycles, and exclude segments the product will not serve in the first release, then write a problem statement in the form of who suffers, what it costs them and how often, and gather evidence such as payment volumes, current settlement times, supplier discount losses and support contacts. Then define the hypotheses, the constraints, the minimum viable product and the success metrics, so discovery ends with a decision rather than with a longer list of ideas.

Discovery ends with a decision, not a longer list.

BA Takeaway

Name the users, exclude the rest, write the problem as who suffers, what it costs and how often, gather the evidence, then define hypotheses, constraints, the minimum viable product and the success metrics.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Target users
→ Excluded segments
→ Problem statement
→ Evidence
→ Hypotheses and constraints
→ MVP and success metrics

The real requirement isn't "How do we make it faster?"

It's "What evidence proves who suffers, what it costs them, and what success looks like?"

Have you ever been asked to make payments faster with no baseline and no target?
takeaway: Define the hypotheses, the constraints, the minimum viable product and the success metrics, so discovery ends with a decision rather than with a longer list of ideas.

title: The supplier file that passes through three screens and a phone call
explain:
A bank runs a legacy supplier payment process that has grown by accretion over a decade.
A corporate customer sends a payment file, operations staff print exception lists, re-key corrected details into three different screens, phone the customer for missing information, and then release the file late in the day.
One file, EUR 45,000 of supplier payments, and a whole afternoon of re-keying.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment file arrives from the customer
→ Exception lists printed
→ Corrected details re-keyed into three screens
→ Customer phoned for missing information
→ File released late in the day

The assumption was:
"Document the process, then improve it."

Begin by observing the work as performed, not as documented: follow real files from intake to release, time each step, and record every workaround, hand-off and re-key, then quantify the pain with measures the business can compare, such as straight-through processing rate, repair rate by defect type, average and worst-case cycle time per step, rework hours, error rate after release and customer contacts per file. Then design the target process, validate the controls and the operational impacts, and only then change the process.

Observe the work as performed, not as documented.

BA Takeaway

Follow real files, time each step, record every workaround and re-key, then quantify the pain before designing anything. The target process is designed from evidence, its controls are validated, and only then does the process change.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Work as performed
→ Straight-through processing rate
→ Repair rate by defect type
→ Cycle time and rework hours
→ Error rate after release

The real requirement isn't "What does the procedure say?"

It's "What evidence proves where the time, the rework and the errors actually sit?"

Have you ever followed a file through a process and found the documented steps bore no relation to the real ones?
takeaway: Design the target process, validate the controls and the operational impacts, and only then change the process.

title: Ten million a month, and the peak is the only number that matters
explain:
Five new clients bring ten million transactions a month, roughly 330,000 a day on average.
The average looks comfortable.
Then payroll and supplier files arrive in concentrated morning windows, and the busiest hour is already at about 70 percent of measured capacity.
The average fits. The peak does not.

Here's how that happens:

→ Ten million a month added
→ 330,000 a day on average
→ Morning file windows concentrate the load
→ Busiest hour already at 70 percent of capacity

The assumption was:
"Plan for the average."

With the busiest hour already at about 70 percent of measured capacity, the only question that matters is whether the peak fits. Convert the growth into throughput, concurrency, queue depth, storage, monitoring and resilience requirements before the clients go live.

Averages hide peaks. Peaks break systems.

BA Takeaway

Size for the peak, not the average. Convert the growth into throughput, concurrency, queue depth, storage, monitoring and resilience requirements, and prove the peak fits before the clients go live.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Measured peak today
→ Added volume at peak
→ Throughput and concurrency
→ Queue depth and storage
→ Monitoring and resilience

The real requirement isn't "How many transactions a month?"

It's "What evidence proves the busiest hour fits inside measured capacity?"

Have you ever signed off capacity on an average, then met the morning peak?
takeaway: Convert the growth into throughput, concurrency, queue depth, storage, monitoring and resilience requirements before the clients go live.

title: One extra hour, and every deadline moves
explain:
The business asks for the customer cut-off to move one hour later.
One hour sounds small.
But a cut-off is not a single time, it is the end of a deadline chain: channel cut-offs, scheme windows, liquidity checks and operational staffing.
Move the hour, and every deadline in the chain moves with it.

Here's how that happens:

→ Cut-off extended by one hour
→ Scheme windows tested
→ Liquidity tested for the extra hour
→ Staffing tested for the later window
→ Exception path for payments that still miss it

The assumption was:
"A cut-off is a single time."

A cut-off is not a single time but the end of a deadline chain, channel cut-offs, scheme windows, liquidity checks and operational staffing. Adding an hour moves the whole chain, and the customer promise has to survive at the new time. Judge the extension on four things, downstream scheme windows, liquidity for the extra hour, staffing to run it, and exception handling for payments that still miss the new cut-off.

A cut-off is the end of a deadline chain.

BA Takeaway

Judge the extension on four things, and prove each one: downstream scheme windows accept the later time, liquidity covers the extra hour, staffing can run the later window, and payments that still miss the new cut-off have a defined exception path.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Downstream scheme windows
→ Liquidity for the extra hour
→ Staffing for the later window
→ Exception handling

The real requirement isn't "Can we move the cut-off?"

It's "What evidence proves the whole deadline chain still holds at the new time?"

Have you ever moved a cut-off by an hour and found every downstream deadline had moved too?
takeaway: Judge the extension on four things, downstream scheme windows, liquidity for the extra hour, staffing to run it, and exception handling for payments that still miss the new cut-off.

title: The rejected direct debit that landed in a third-party account
explain:
A direct debit collection of EUR 9,500 is rejected by the debtor bank.
Normally it returns to the creditor bank, authorising it to debit the originator's account.
This time the collection is booked to a designated third-party account instead, and the operations team is not sure the booking was ever allowed.

Here's how that happens:

→ Collection rejected by the debtor bank
→ Normal path returns it to the creditor bank
→ Third-party account proposed instead
→ Preconditions checked, or skipped?

The assumption was:
"A reject always goes back the way it came."

A debtor bank normally returns a rejected collection to the creditor bank, authorising it to debit the originator's account, but a collection can instead be booked to a designated third-party account. The third-party account is funded to meet regulatory obligations and to follow rejected payments through the general ledger, and it can be used only if the originator's instructions allow it, the account was opened and funded first, and it is opened and maintained by the creditor bank. Building it as a system requirement is a sensitive decision that needs product owner and business owner agreement, with checks for the returning customer, fraud signs and valid repayment flows.

A third-party account for rejects is a sensitive decision, not a routing option.

BA Takeaway

Challenge the requirement before building it. The account can be used only if the originator's instructions allow it, the account was opened and funded first, and the creditor bank opens and maintains it, with product owner and business owner agreement, and checks for the returning customer, fraud signs and valid repayment flows.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Originator instruction allows it
→ Account opened and funded first
→ Creditor bank opens and maintains it
→ Product and business owner agreement
→ Fraud and repayment checks

The real requirement isn't "Can we book it there?"

It's "What evidence proves the originator allowed it, the account was funded first, and the owners agreed?"

Have you ever been asked to build a routing option that turned out to be a sensitive decision in disguise?
takeaway: A BA cannot necessarily refuse a requirement, yet challenging it remains the BA responsibility.

title: The consent arrived late. The 500 payments were still moving.
explain:
A set of 500 payments is being cancelled.
A negative camt.029 arrives while the payment engine is still processing the set.
Then a beneficiary consent arrives, after the expected timeframe, for payments that may already be on their way back.

Here's how that happens:

→ camt.056 cancels the payment set
→ Negative camt.029 arrives mid-processing
→ Late beneficiary consent arrives
→ pacs.004 return follows, per payment or grouped

The assumption was:
"Late consent is just late."

A negative camt.029 can arrive while a payment engine is still processing a set of 500 payments, and a beneficiary consent can then arrive after the expected timeframe, while the pacs.004 return that follows can be made per payment or grouped by customer, reason, value or compliance cause. The remaining payments have no universal answer: return them, complete them, or reject the late consent by accepting or overriding the rule, so each bank must define when a late consent can be accepted and when it cannot, and record the message, the consent and the retention rules that apply. Treating a late consent as merely late misses the point, since it can still reflect sound business behaviour.

Treating a late consent as merely late misses the point.

BA Takeaway

Define the bank rule for late consent in writing: when it can be accepted, when it cannot, and what is recorded, the message, the consent and the retention rules. A late consent can still reflect sound business behaviour, and the remaining payments are returned, completed or rejected by that rule, not by habit.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Bank rule for late consent
→ Message recorded
→ Consent recorded
→ Retention rules applied

The real requirement isn't "Was the consent late?"

It's "What evidence proves the bank rule allows this consent, and what was recorded?"

Have you ever received a consent after the deadline and had to decide whether it still counted?
takeaway: Treating a late consent as merely late misses the point, since it can still reflect sound business behaviour.

title: ISO 20022 ready? Eight gaps say otherwise
explain:
A bank is migrating to ISO 20022, and the project plan says the business is ready.
The messages are mapped, the build is on track, and the go-live date is set.
Then the first customer payment journey breaks, because nobody aligned the processes, the hand-offs, the training, the data quality or the control teams.

Here's how that happens:

→ Messages mapped, build on track
→ Processes not aligned to customer journeys
→ Hand-offs unplanned, teams untrained
→ Systems cannot hold high data quality
→ Compliance, fraud and AML not aligned

The assumption was:
"Migration is a message format change."

ISO 20022 migration is a transformation of the payments business model, not a message format change, and readiness fails where processes are not aligned to customer payment journeys, hand-offs are unplanned, business teams are untrained, systems cannot hold high data quality, and compliance, fraud and AML teams are not aligned. Limited resources, missing governance and weak coordination across stakeholders leave the gap between business and technology in place even after execution starts.

ISO 20022 migration is a transformation of the payments business model, not a message format change.

BA Takeaway

Close the eight gaps before claiming readiness: journey alignment, planned hand-offs, trained business teams, high data quality, aligned control teams, and governance, resources and coordination across stakeholders.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Journey alignment
→ Planned hand-offs
→ Trained business teams
→ High data quality
→ Aligned control teams
→ Governance and resources

The real requirement isn't "Are the messages mapped?"

It's "What evidence proves the business, not just the build, is ready?"

Have you ever watched a migration go live with the messages ready and the business unready?
takeaway: A migration plan must close these eight gaps before it can claim the business is ready.

title: Blockchain for payments: four questions nobody has closed
explain:
A EUR 40,000 payment is proposed on a shared ledger, and the room is full of confidence.
Then four questions land, and nobody in the room can answer any of them.
Who sees the confidential fields? Who maintains the ledger? What format does it use? And can one network really span domestic and cross-border payments?

Here's how that happens:

→ Shared ledger proposed for payments
→ Confidential fields visible to every node
→ Formats vary by network
→ One network proposed for domestic and cross-border

The assumption was:
"Blockchain answers everything at once."

Transparency means every node sees transaction detail, and control over confidential fields is still being built. A business relationship links each node with every other node, which simplifies maintenance of the shared ledger. Formats will vary with the algorithm each network uses, so one universal message and ledger format is ambitious yet not impossible. A single network spanning domestic and cross-border payments is achievable if the industry aligns on common standards.

A single network spanning domestic and cross-border payments is achievable if the industry aligns on common standards.

BA Takeaway

Answer the four questions before proposing the ledger: confidentiality of fields, the business relationships between nodes, the message and ledger formats, and the common standards a single network would need.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Confidentiality
→ Business relationships
→ Formats
→ Reach

The real requirement isn't "Can we use blockchain?"

It's "What evidence proves the four open questions have answers?"

Have you ever sat in a room where a new technology was proposed and the basic questions had no answers?
takeaway: A single network spanning domestic and cross-border payments is achievable if the industry aligns on common standards.

explain:
GBP 40,000 left London for a supplier overseas.
The customer was told the payment was sent.
The supplier was never paid.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank
→ MT103 passes sanctions screening
→ MT202 COV held at an intermediary bank
→ Beneficiary bank waits for the cover
→ No credit is made

The assumption said:
"Screen the MT103. The cover follows the same path."

So only the information leg was screened, and the funds leg was left to travel on trust.

Why?

An MT103 and its MT202 COV are screened separately, and a hit on either leg stops the payment. The intermediary held the cover for sanctions screening while the MT103 had already arrived, so the beneficiary bank had the instruction and no money to pay with.

A clear MT103 is not a paid beneficiary.

Screening the information leg does not clear the funds leg.

BA Takeaway

The MT103 is information. The cover is the money.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT103 screening status
→ MT202 COV screening status
→ Funds received and reconciled

Never tell a customer a payment is sent until both legs are clear.

The real requirement is not "When do we send the MT103?"

It is "What evidence proves both legs are clear and the money can move?"

Have you seen a payment marked sent while the cover was still held?
takeaway: The MT103 is information. The cover is the money. Screening one does not clear the other.

explain:
A correspondent cut its intraday credit limit without warning.
The payment engine kept feeding the same corridor.
By the afternoon, payments were queuing, then rejecting, and nobody could explain why.

Here is how that happens:

→ Correspondent cuts the intraday limit
→ Engine keeps sending at the old volume
→ Queue builds on the corridor
→ Payments reject with no clear reason
→ Operations cannot reconstruct which payments were affected

The assumption said:
"Routing rules are written for the quiet day."

So the rules had no eligibility check, no fallback route and no audit trail, and the bad day arrived exactly as it always does, without warning.

Why?

A correspondent can cut an intraday credit limit without warning, and an engine that keeps feeding the same corridor will queue payments and generate rejects it cannot explain. Routing decisions must carry eligibility checks, fallback routes, a defined decision order and an audit trail naming the affected payments and the reason.

A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control failure.

The queue was not the failure. The silence about the queue was.

BA Takeaway

Build routing rules for the bad day, not the quiet one.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Eligibility check before routing
→ Fallback route when a limit is cut
→ Defined decision order
→ Audit trail naming every affected payment

The real requirement is not "Which route is fastest?"

It is "What evidence proves this route is still open, and what happens if it closes?"

Have you seen a corridor fail while the engine kept feeding it?
takeaway: Build routing rules for the bad day, not the quiet one. A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control failure.

explain:
A cover payment settled cleanly months ago.
Then an MT191 arrived, claiming the intermediary charges.
The nostro was debited, reconciliation broke, and nobody remembered the payment.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT103 and MT202 COV settle in full
→ Intermediary is owed charges for its part in the chain
→ Intermediary claims them separately by MT191
→ Nostro debited months after the payment
→ Reconciliation breaks on a payment everyone had closed

The assumption said:
"Charges are taken from the payment. There is nothing left to claim."

So the team closed the books on the payment and never expected the charges leg to arrive on its own timetable.

Why?

Charges must never be deducted from a cover payment, so an intermediary that is owed money asks for it separately instead of taking it from the funds. The claim travels in an MT191, a request for payment of charges, and the advice travels in an MT190. A reader who sees an MT191 in a chain is looking at the charges leg, not the payment itself.

The cover is not the charges leg.

The payment settled. The bill for moving it arrived later.

BA Takeaway

A cover that arrives short is an exception. The charges travel separately.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cover amount, never reduced for charges
→ Charges claimed by MT191
→ Charges advised by MT190
→ Nostro reconciliation that expects late claims

The real requirement is not "Did the cover arrive in full?"

It is "What evidence proves every charge in the chain was claimed, advised and reconciled?"

takeaway: The cover is not the charges leg. Charges travel separately, by MT191, and can arrive months later.

explain:
A cross-border payment needed sterling settlement in the UK.
The sterling leg went by CHAPS, for a house purchase completion that day.
The completion missed its day.

Here is how that happens:

→ MT103 arrives for the cross-border payment
→ Sterling leg sent to CHAPS
→ Payment queued for insufficient liquidity
→ Customer cut-off passes with the payment still queued
→ Settlement moves to the next working day

The assumption said:
"CHAPS settles the same day. Send it and the completion is safe."

So the team promised the day without checking the balance behind it, and without remembering that the cross-border leg still needed its own route out of the UK.

Why?

CHAPS settles sterling payments between UK banks in central bank money, and a cross-border payment that needs sterling settlement in the UK can use it as the domestic leg. But CHAPS settles the same day only during business hours and only with liquidity behind the payment. A payment queued for insufficient funds waits, and the customer cut-off passes while it waits.

Same day is a promise with a cut-off and a balance behind it.

CHAPS was one leg of the journey, not the whole journey.

BA Takeaway

A CHAPS leg needs liquidity confirmed before the customer is promised the day.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Liquidity available for the CHAPS leg
→ Customer cut-off, checked before promising the day
→ Cross-border leg, routed separately out of the UK
→ Queued payment, watched until it settles

The real requirement is not "Can CHAPS settle today?"

It is "What evidence proves the funds, the cut-off and the onward route all line up today?"

Have you seen a same-day promise fail on a queued CHAPS payment?
takeaway: Same day is a promise with a cut-off and a balance behind it. Confirm liquidity before promising the day.

explain:
A EUR 5 million payment was accepted on Monday for Friday execution.
The customer was promised Friday.
On Thursday, the beneficiary was added to a sanctions list.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment accepted Monday for Friday execution
→ Payment warehoused until Friday
→ Sanctions list changes on Thursday
→ Friday revalidation checks sanctions status
→ Execution blocked, customer promise broken

The assumption said:
"Valid on Monday means valid on Friday."

So the team treated warehousing as storage, and forgot that four days is enough for the world to change.

Why?

Warehousing turns a future-dated payment into a commitment to execute, not merely a stored instruction. Balance, account details, sanctions status and cut-off times can all move between submission and execution, so validity on Monday proves nothing about Friday. The payment must be re-validated on balance, account status, sanctions and cut-offs at execution, then executed or rejected.

Warehousing stores the promise, not the permission.

Monday's checks were perfect. Friday's world was different.

BA Takeaway

Re-validate at execution. Monday's checks prove nothing about Friday.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Validity at submission
→ Validity at execution, checked again
→ Sanctions status on the execution day
→ Balance and cut-off, checked again

The real requirement is not "Was it valid when accepted?"

It is "What evidence proves it is still valid on the day it moves?"

takeaway: Warehousing stores the promise, not the permission. Re-validate at execution.

explain:
A customer with a EUR 300,000 limit sent EUR 200,000 instantly.
It did not arrive instantly.
It travelled to TARGET2 instead, slower and costlier.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer sends EUR 200,000 by SCT Inst
→ Routing rule sees an amount above EUR 100,000
→ Payment routed to TARGET2
→ Arrives later, at TARGET2 cost
→ Customer asks why the instant payment was not instant

The assumption said:
"The routing rule follows the scheme limit."

So the rule kept enforcing a limit the scheme had already removed, and two live rules produced different outcomes for the same payment.

Why?

When the EU Instant Payments Regulation removed the EUR 100,000 scheme-level maximum for SCT Inst, the old routing rule that sent payments above EUR 100,000 to TARGET2 lost the scheme limit it was built on. A bank can now set its own customer limits, so a customer with a EUR 300,000 limit can send EUR 200,000 instantly while the unchanged routing rule still sends anything above EUR 100,000 to TARGET2.

A rule built on a dead limit is a live defect.

The scheme moved on. The routing rule did not.

BA Takeaway

When a scheme limit dies, every rule built on it must be re-checked.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme limit, as it stands today
→ Customer limit, set by the bank
→ Routing rule, traced to the limit it was built on
→ Conflict check when any limit changes

The real requirement is not "What does the routing rule say?"

It is "What evidence proves the routing rule still matches the scheme and the customer limit?"

Have you seen a payment take the slow route because a rule outlived its limit?
takeaway: A rule built on a dead limit is a live defect. When a scheme limit dies, re-check every rule built on it.

explain:
A cross-border payment was promised in 60 seconds.
The euro leg cleared on time.
The beneficiary was paid late, and short of the expected amount.

Here is how that happens:

→ OCT Inst payment starts in Europe
→ Euro leg clears and settles in seconds
→ Non-euro leg conversion runs outside the euro area
→ Conversion is not complete before the beneficiary is due
→ Beneficiary paid late, for less than expected

The assumption said:
"Sixty seconds covers the whole payment."

So the team sold the headline time and forgot that the second leg lives under different rules, different standards and different bank policies.

Why?

OCT Inst processes cross-border payments in 60 seconds, handling both the payment and the settlement, with both legs settled through the euro system. But the non-euro leg runs wholly outside the euro area, governed by non-euro rules, standards and bank policies, with conversion completed before the beneficiary is paid, so the beneficiary receives exactly the amount expected. Speed is not the test here, reliability and rule-following are.

Speed is not the test. Reliability and rule-following are.

The euro leg was instant. The payment was not.

BA Takeaway

The 60-second promise ends where the non-euro leg begins. Prove the conversion first.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Euro leg, cleared in seconds
→ Non-euro leg, governed by non-euro rules
→ Conversion complete before the beneficiary is paid
→ Exact amount the beneficiary will receive, confirmed

The real requirement is not "How fast is the euro leg?"

It is "What evidence proves the conversion is done and the beneficiary gets the exact amount?"

takeaway: Speed is not the test. Reliability and rule-following are. Prove the conversion before promising 60 seconds.
